# The Department of Unfinished Things

On her first morning at the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was given a brass key, a cup with somebody else’s name on it, and a warning about the third floor.

“Nothing dangerous,” said the director. “But you may hear applause.”

The department occupied an old municipal building between the tax office and a shop that sold only lampshades. Its windows were tall and perpetually dusty. Above the entrance, someone had carved a sentence into the stone, then abandoned it halfway through:

*FOR THE BENEFIT OF ALL WHO*

Mara had applied because the advertisement promised regular hours and no public speaking. Her previous job involved explaining parking regulations to people who believed their circumstances were unique.

“What exactly do we keep here?” she asked.

The director, whose name was Ivo, opened a drawer.

Inside lay a blue mitten with three fingers.

“Things people meant to finish.”

“All of them?”

“Good heavens, no. We have six employees.”

He closed the drawer gently.

“We keep the ones that arrive.”

This seemed to Mara like a distinction designed to prevent further questions. She would eventually learn that it was the department’s only workable philosophy.

Her desk stood beside a window overlooking a narrow courtyard. Someone had begun planting a garden there years ago. Six neat rows of labels emerged from the soil, naming vegetables that had never appeared.

At noon, she washed the borrowed cup.

The name on it was Daniel.

She wondered whether he had left, or simply stopped coming.

---

Things arrived by post, by hand, and occasionally through mechanisms no one could explain.

A half-written cookbook appeared inside the locked stationery cupboard. A staircase leading nowhere materialized overnight in the basement. Every Thursday, the department received one additional sentence of a detective novel whose author had been dead for nineteen years.

The sentences were not especially good.

“We don’t assess quality,” Ivo told her.

Mara’s work was to enter each arrival in a ledger, describe its condition, and assign it a shelf.

Some items were easy.

*One wool scarf, green, approximately two-thirds complete.*

Others required judgment.

*An apology beginning with an explanation of why the writer was actually the injured party.*

“Correspondence?” Mara asked.

“Structural failures,” said Ivo.

There were abandoned business plans, model ships without rigging, lullabies missing their last lines, and thousands of notebooks whose first pages announced ambitious new lives.

One entire room contained language courses.

Another held exercise equipment, though the department had stopped accepting that in March.

What surprised Mara was how tenderly everything had been packed. Even the most hopeless manuscript arrived wrapped against the rain. Even the ugliest clay bowl had been cushioned with newspaper.

People might surrender their intentions, but they rarely did so without ceremony.

On Friday, she found a small envelope addressed simply:

*To whoever can bear to look.*

Inside was a drawing of a horse.

Only the head was finished.

It was a very good head.

Mara stood it against her lamp instead of filing it immediately.

---

The applause began during her second week.

It drifted down the stairwell at four seventeen: a great soft thunder, followed by the unmistakable sound of a crowd rising to its feet.

Mara looked up.

No one else moved.

“Third floor,” said Tomas, who repaired the department’s clocks despite none of them belonging to the department.

“What’s up there?”

“Things that were almost done.”

“That sounds encouraging.”

“Sometimes.”

He was a narrow old man with a watchmaker’s lens permanently lodged above one eyebrow. Before retirement, he had tuned pianos. He now came three days a week because, he said, his apartment was too quiet and the library too warm.

He took her upstairs.

The third floor contained a concert hall barely larger than a classroom. On its stage stood an upright piano. Beside it rested a pair of shoes, polished so thoroughly that they seemed wet.

“There was a woman,” Tomas said. “She practiced for eleven years. Had a recital booked. Invitations printed.”

“What happened?”

“She didn’t go.”

“Why?”

“We don’t usually get the why.”

Mara approached the piano. A sheet of music lay open on its stand. The final measure was blank.

“Does the applause bother you?” Tomas asked.

“A little.”

“It used to bother me.”

“What changed?”

He considered this.

“I stopped assuming they were applauding the performance.”

They stood together until the hall fell silent.

Then Tomas bent down and straightened one of the shoes, which had turned slightly toward the door.

---

A month after Mara arrived, the city announced that the department would close.

The building required repairs. The collection had no measurable public value. The lampshade shop wished to expand.

Ivo read the letter twice, then placed it in the tray marked PENDING, which struck Mara as either defiance or habit.

“How long?” she asked.

“Thirty days.”

“What happens to everything?”

“The instructions say disposal.”

Outside, a delivery van reversed into the alley, beeping cheerfully.

For the first time, Mara found the arrivals irritating. Another box of someone’s abandoned enthusiasm. Another claim on shelves that would soon cease to exist.

She carried it inside with less care than usual.

The box contained a wooden boat.

Not a model. A real boat, somehow folded into a parcel smaller than a suitcase. When she lifted it free, it expanded across three desks, scattering pencils.

Its hull was painted yellow. One side was smooth; the other remained rough timber. A paper label hung from the bow.

*For Mara, when she is old enough.*

She recognized the handwriting before she understood the words.

Her father had been dead for fourteen years.

She touched the yellow paint. Beneath her finger was a ridge where a drip had dried.

She remembered that drip.

She remembered standing in his workshop, asking whether the boat would be ready by summer.

She remembered asking again the following summer.

Ivo appeared beside her.

“Oh,” he said.

For once, he offered no administrative clarification.

---

Her father had been a man of projects.

He built shelves, repaired bicycles, bought seeds, sketched extensions to houses he did not own. He could make a child feel that next Saturday would contain everything missing from the world.

Next Saturday they would test the boat.

Next Saturday they would drive to the sea.

Next Saturday he would explain the stars.

He was loving, funny, and late. Mara had spent years defending the first two qualities against the third, as if affection were a court case in which only one verdict could be returned.

After he died, other people remembered his generosity.

Mara remembered waiting in a coat.

This had made grief feel impolite.

She walked around the boat. On the unfinished side, pencil marks indicated where another plank should go. A small nail had been tapped into place and left standing, waiting for the next blow.

“Can things be claimed?” she asked.

“Certainly,” Ivo said.

“By anyone?”

“By the person they belong to.”

“And how do you establish that?”

He looked at the label.

“Sometimes the evidence is overwhelming.”

She did not claim it.

Instead, she assigned it a number and moved it into the room reserved for domestic inventions.

For the rest of the afternoon she catalogued a half-built bread oven, three incomplete family trees, and a system for organizing kitchen drawers that consisted entirely of a furious preface.

At closing time, she went back to the boat.

It had not changed.

She found this both reassuring and unfair.

---

The next morning, Mara proposed opening the department to the public.

“People can take their things back.”

Ivo glanced at the closure letter.

“The city asked for a disposal plan.”

“This is one.”

“Possibly.”

“We could call it redistribution.”

“That is much better.”

They put a notice in the newspaper. Tomas made a sign. Someone from Records found a kettle large enough to suggest hospitality on an institutional scale.

On Saturday, a queue formed before opening.

The first visitor was a woman looking for a red cardigan she had begun knitting during her pregnancy. Her son came with her. He was thirty-two and carried the kettle inside.

A man arrived for a screenplay and left it there after reading seven pages.

“I was very angry,” he said, almost admiringly.

A girl collected a science fair volcano. An elderly couple reclaimed a dance they had stopped learning when one of them broke an ankle.

The dance required some space.

For several minutes, everyone in the entrance hall moved aside.

Not every reunion was happy.

One woman found a letter from her brother and asked why the department had not sent it years ago.

Ivo explained, quietly, that they were not a postal service.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

She took the letter anyway.

By afternoon, Mara’s voice was hoarse. Her hands smelled of dust and tea.

The shelves were visibly emptier.

For the first time since the closure notice, the work seemed possible again.

---

On the ninth day, Mara’s mother came.

She wore her good coat and carried an umbrella, although there was no rain.

“I saw the notice,” she said.

Mara had not told her about the boat.

Now she led her through the rooms without knowing whether she wanted a witness, an explanation, or someone else to be blamed.

Her mother stood beside the yellow hull for a long time.

“He worked on this after you went to bed.”

“I know.”

“Sometimes until one.”

“I know.”

Her mother touched the unfinished timber.

“He wanted it to be perfect.”

Mara felt the old defense assembling itself around them.

“I wanted it to float.”

Her mother withdrew her hand.

From somewhere upstairs came a few tentative notes on the piano.

“Yes,” she said finally. “You did.”

They stood in the awkward silence that follows when a family’s familiar story acquires a sentence it cannot absorb.

Then her mother opened her handbag.

“I came for something else.”

She produced a receipt dated twenty-three years earlier.

The corresponding shelf held a letter addressed to Mara’s father.

Her mother read it, folded it, and laughed once.

“What does it say?”

“That I was leaving him.”

Mara stared.

“Were you?”

“I was furious. I wrote six pages. Then I went downstairs to tell him instead.”

“What happened?”

“We talked.”

Her mother returned the letter to its envelope.

“Some things aren’t finished because you find a better way to do them.”

She slipped it into her pocket.

---

As the deadline approached, the department changed its rules.

People could adopt things that had never belonged to them, provided they understood that ownership did not include the obligation to fulfill a stranger’s dream.

A teacher took the unfinished horse for her classroom.

A carpenter collected the staircase to nowhere.

“What will you do with it?” Mara asked.

“Make it go somewhere.”

“That seems obvious now you’ve said it.”

The detective novel went to a reading group willing to argue about the ending. The language courses went to a neighborhood center. Most were probably destined to remain incomplete, but they would at least be incomplete in company.

Other items required more caution.

They did not redistribute apologies. Promises, Ivo ruled, could not be transferred without the consent of the person to whom they had been made.

Nor could the department excuse unpaid wages, neglected children, or damage that someone had found inconvenient to repair.

Those files went to offices whose windows were less dusty and whose powers were more concrete.

“An abandoned symphony is one thing,” Ivo said. “An abandoned responsibility is another.”

Mara wrote this on a card beside the entrance.

The applause upstairs grew less frequent.

One afternoon, the polished shoes disappeared. No one saw who collected them.

Tomas tuned the piano for the first and last time.

When he finished, he played a tune Mara almost recognized.

“Is that complete?” she asked.

“Oh yes.”

“How can you tell?”

He lifted his hands.

“Because that’s where I stop.”

---

On the final evening, only a few things remained.

A weather machine that produced drizzle. A portrait with no face. Seventeen introductions to books about discipline.

And the boat.

Mara sat inside it with her knees raised. It smelled faintly of sawdust, despite all the years that should have carried that smell away.

For a while, she tried to imagine finishing it.

She could take a class. Buy tools. Learn the difference between wood that tolerated water and wood that merely looked confident.

She could spend weekends completing the gift.

The thought exhausted her.

Then she tried to imagine destroying it.

That felt like another kind of assignment.

Tomas found her there.

“You don’t have to decide tonight,” he said.

“The building closes tomorrow.”

“The building does.”

She ran a hand along the gunwale.

“If I finish it, it feels like I’m saying it was all right.”

“And if you don’t?”

“It feels like I’m still waiting.”

Tomas leaned against a desk.

“Those are two possibilities.”

“Do you have a third?”

“No. But there are usually more than two.”

After he left, Mara stayed until the courtyard darkened.

Through the window she could see the rows of labels in the empty garden.

BEANS.

CARROTS.

PEAS.

She pictured the boat out there in the sunlight, filled with soil. The idea was almost ridiculous enough to phone her father about.

She sat with that impulse until it passed.

Then she went downstairs to find the handcart and measure the courtyard gate.

---

The lampshade shop kept the courtyard.

Mara negotiated this during the handover, along with access through the side gate and permission to remove the vegetable labels.

The owner agreed.

“I’ve always wanted somewhere to eat lunch.”

They carried the boat outside with help from the carpenter. He drilled drainage holes in the bottom, a procedure that made Mara wince and then laugh.

Her mother brought compost.

Tomas brought seedlings in paper cups.

Ivo arrived with the old brass key, which he insisted should remain with someone who knew what it opened.

They planted lavender, nasturtiums, and strawberries.

Nothing symbolic, Mara told them. Things that would survive the weather.

By June, the yellow hull had begun to fade. Bees moved through the lavender. The lampshade seller ate sandwiches beside the stern and occasionally remembered to water.

Mara visited on Thursdays.

Some weeks she missed.

The garden endured this ordinary imperfection.

One afternoon, a child peered through the gate and asked why there was a boat full of dirt.

“It doesn’t go on the water,” Mara said.

“Is it broken?”

She considered the question.

“It was never finished.”

The child looked at the leaves spilling over its side.

“Looks finished.”

Mara smiled.

From the street came a bicycle bell, a delivery truck, two people disagreeing about directions. Somewhere, someone was beginning something they would not complete.

She picked a strawberry and offered it through the bars.

The child ate it, then pointed to another, still white beneath its leaves.

“Not yet,” Mara said.
